Seam carving

Content-aware resizing: interactive resize, method comparison, benchmarks and tests.

ResizeMethodsBenchmarksTests

Interactive resize

Every vertical seam is computed once by the C++ program (DP, L1 energy) on the full-resolution picture; each step of the slider cuts one more of them. Images run from easiest to hardest, measured by the average energy of the pixels the DP carve removes: low means there was plenty of flat background to take away.

Methods on the same input

All panels start from the same input, shrunk to at most 320 px wide, and remove 50% of its width. Removed energy is the sum of seam costs (lower is better); baselines have no seams. Times come from the demo run, which processes the images in parallel, so they are indicative only; the benchmarks below are the controlled measurements.

Benchmarks

The benchmarks answer three questions from the brief, one group each. Every time is the median of 5 timed runs after 1 warm-up, built with -O2.

  1. How does the cost grow with image size? (5b, 2a, 2b) Line charts on log-log axes: a straight line means a power law, and its slope is the exponent, so slope 2 means the time grows with the number of pixels n x n.
  2. Do the improvements help? (5d) Bar charts: each compares two to four ways of doing the same job on the same input.
  3. How do the methods compare on a real carve? (3, 4, 5c) A table of whole carves to 50% width: time and the total energy removed (lower is better).

Tests

Every test checks its result by an independent route (brute force, a second algorithm, a hand-computed table or a max-flow certificate).
